ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated multi-task learning through a shared public-data representation space
PROPOSAL: We let each user keep an arbitrary encoder and task head, and coordinate only through embeddings of a small unlabelled public dataset that every user computes locally and sends to the server. The server learns a joint alignment objective over all users' embeddings at once, returns per-user alignment targets, and each user adds an alignment loss to its local task loss. We test on a benchmark mixing image classification, segmentation and text classification users with different backbones, including fine-tuned foundation models.
CONTROLS: Local training only, pairwise contrastive alignment between every pair of users, distillation on public logits restricted to same-task users, and a centered kernel alignment proximal term.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: Joint alignment should beat local training for most users and beat pairwise alignment when users number more than three. Users whose tasks share little with the rest may see no gain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A volume-based contrastive loss for aligning many models at once
PROPOSAL: We propose a contrastive objective that treats the embeddings of one instance from all models as the columns of a matrix and rewards small volume of that matrix for positives relative to negatives, and we derive it as a lower bound on the total correlation among all representations. This gives a theoretical footing to Gramian-style alignment. We evaluate representation quality by linear probing on each model's task and by retrieval across models, with three to eight participating models.
CONTROLS: Pairwise contrastive alignment over all pairs, the existing Gramian loss without our normalisation, and independent training, with the number of models varied to show how each loss scales.
COST: 340
PREDICTION: The volume objective should match pairwise alignment with three models and pull ahead as more models join. The bound may become loose for very high-dimensional embeddings, reducing the advantage there.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Communication-efficient alignment by exchanging compressed public embeddings
PROPOSAL: We reduce the communication of representation-based federated multi-task learning by sending low-precision, randomly projected embeddings of public data instead of full ones, and by refreshing alignment targets only every few rounds. We characterise the trade-off between bytes exchanged and accuracy for users with heterogeneous architectures and tasks, and compare against parameter-sharing methods that need congruent encoders.
CONTROLS: Full-precision embeddings exchanged every round, parameter sharing of a common encoder where architectures allow it, and local training, with total uploaded bytes per user tracked alongside task metrics.
COST: 250
PREDICTION: Compressed embeddings should lose little accuracy while cutting traffic well below that of parameter sharing. Aggressive projection could collapse fine-grained structure needed by dense prediction tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-modal collaboration between image, text and audio users without shared parameters
PROPOSAL: We study users in different modalities who share a public paired dataset of images, captions and audio clips. Each user embeds only its own modality, and the server aligns all embeddings of the same public instance jointly, so knowledge moves between an image classifier, a text sentiment model and a speech command recogniser that never exchange weights. We measure each user's task accuracy against training on local data alone.
CONTROLS: Local training only, pairwise contrastive alignment between modalities, and a heuristic multi-modal regularisation method designed for two modalities, extended to three by summing its pairwise terms.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: Joint alignment should improve every user, with the largest gains for the user with the smallest local dataset. Without enough public paired data the alignment targets will be noisy and the benefit will shrink.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Privacy leakage of sharing public-data embeddings compared with sharing parameters
PROPOSAL: We quantify how much information about local training data leaks through the public-data embeddings that representation-based federated methods exchange, and compare it with leakage from shared encoder parameters. We run membership inference and attribute inference attacks against users with different architectures and tasks, using open image and text datasets as local data.
CONTROLS: Attacks on a user that shares nothing as a floor, attacks on parameter-sharing federated methods, and embeddings with added noise at several levels to trace the trade-off between accuracy and leakage.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: Embedding sharing should leak less than parameter sharing at equal accuracy. Users fine-tuned heavily on small datasets may still leak membership through their public-data embeddings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: When does cross-task transfer help in federated multi-task learning
PROPOSAL: We vary task relatedness systematically across users, from identical tasks to unrelated ones, by constructing user tasks from controlled splits of a large labelled image corpus, and measure the gain of joint representation alignment over local training for each user as a function of relatedness and local data size. Each user picks its architecture from a pool of convolutional and transformer backbones.
CONTROLS: Local training, a centralised upper reference that pools all data, and alignment with shuffled public instances as placebo.
COST: 290
PREDICTION: Gains should be largest for related tasks and small local datasets, and fall towards zero for unrelated tasks. Negative transfer may appear when one dominant user pulls the shared space towards its own task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Server-side aggregation of alignment targets weighted by user agreement
PROPOSAL: We replace uniform averaging of public-data embeddings on the server by a weighting in which each user's contribution to the alignment target grows with its agreement with the other users on held-out public instances. This should limit the influence of users with poor or unrelated representations. We test with users of different architectures, including some with very little local data and some with noisy labels.
CONTROLS: Uniform averaging, median aggregation, local training, and a setting where the low-quality users are removed entirely as an upper reference.
COST: 230
PREDICTION: Agreement weighting should recover most of the gain of removing low-quality users without needing to identify them. If all users are weak, the weighting will have nothing reliable to anchor on.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling joint alignment to dozens of heterogeneous users
PROPOSAL: We study how joint representation alignment behaves as the number of federated users grows from four to sixty-four, with users drawn from a pool of tasks and architectures and with partial participation in each round. We track per-user accuracy, convergence speed and the server computation required by the joint loss, and compare with pairwise schemes whose cost grows with the square of the number of users.
CONTROLS: Pairwise contrastive alignment, local training, and joint alignment with the number of users fixed at four to isolate the effect of scale.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: Joint alignment should keep improving or hold accuracy as users increase, while pairwise schemes become impractical. Partial participation could slow convergence when few users share a task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated collaboration among users who fine-tune different foundation models
PROPOSAL: We simulate users who each select a different pretrained foundation model according to their resources, from small convolutional networks to large vision transformers, and adapt it on a few local examples for their own task. Collaboration uses only alignment on public-data embeddings. We measure whether small-model users benefit from the representations of large-model users and whether large-model users lose anything.
CONTROLS: Local fine-tuning, distillation from the largest model on same-task users only, and alignment where the large model is frozen, to see whether its gains come from receiving or from giving.
COST: 650
PREDICTION: Small-model users should gain the most, and large-model users should hold their accuracy. A large capacity gap may make alignment targets hard for small models to follow.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Testing whether total-correlation alignment captures higher-order dependence
PROPOSAL: We construct synthetic multi-view data in which three views are pairwise independent but jointly dependent, so that only an objective sensitive to higher-order dependence can align them. We train encoders with pairwise contrastive losses and with a joint total-correlation objective and test which recovers the shared latent variable.
CONTROLS: Pairwise losses over all pairs, the joint objective, random encoders, and a version of the data with only pairwise dependence where both objectives should succeed.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: Only the joint objective should recover the latent in the higher-order setting. Optimisation difficulties may prevent it from doing so reliably with small batches.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint public-data alignment for users with different architectures and tasks
PROPOSAL: Users keep arbitrary encoders and task heads and share only embeddings of an unlabelled public dataset, which the server aligns jointly across all users before returning per-user targets. Whether this transfers knowledge across tasks without architectural congruity is tested on users mixing image classification, segmentation and text tasks.
CONTROLS: Local training as the floor, a centralised model on pooled data as the ceiling, pairwise contrastive alignment over all pairs, distillation on public logits for same-task users, a kernel alignment proximal term, and alignment on shuffled public instances as placebo, over three seeds.
COST: 520
PREDICTION: Joint alignment should beat local training for most users and beat pairwise alignment beyond three users. If the placebo helps as much, the gain does not come from shared structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Public-data alignment for a federation of heterogeneous users
PROPOSAL: Users keep arbitrary encoders and task heads and share only embeddings of an unlabelled public dataset, which the server aligns jointly across all users before returning per-user targets. We run the scheme on users mixing image classification, segmentation and text tasks, reporting each user's accuracy after training.
CONTROLS: The scheme with two public dataset sizes, two embedding dimensions on the server, an ablation of the server learning rate, a check of training curves for each user, and per-user accuracy against the numbers reported for each backbone in its original paper.
COST: 520
PREDICTION: Each user should reach accuracy close to that reported for its backbone. Users with very small local data may lag behind the others.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Is the volume-based loss a better joint aligner than pairwise contrastive losses
PROPOSAL: We train representations of the same instances across several models with a volume-based contrastive loss derived as a bound on their total correlation, and test it against pairwise alternatives on synthetic data with known dependence and on real multi-view benchmarks, varying the number of models from three to eight.
CONTROLS: Pairwise InfoNCE summed over all pairs, the Gramian loss without theoretical normalisation, independent training, synthetic views with higher-order dependence only, and linear probing plus cross-model retrieval as metrics.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: The volume loss should win clearly when dependence is higher-order and as models grow in number. If pairwise losses match it on the synthetic data, the theoretical motivation adds nothing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training a volume-based contrastive loss on multi-view benchmarks
PROPOSAL: We train representations of the same instances across several models with a volume-based contrastive loss derived as a bound on their total correlation, and report retrieval and probing quality on real multi-view benchmarks with three to eight models, along with training curves for the loss.
CONTROLS: Two temperature values for the loss, an ablation of embedding normalisation, the loss trained with two batch sizes, embeddings visualised with a two-dimensional projection, and linear probing plus cross-model retrieval as metrics.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: The volume loss should produce aligned embeddings across all views. Larger batch sizes may improve retrieval because of more negatives per update.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring the communication savings of embedding-based collaboration
PROPOSAL: We compress the public-data embeddings exchanged in representation-based federated learning with random projection and quantisation, and quantify bytes exchanged against accuracy for each heterogeneous user, to answer whether collaboration of this kind stays practical.
CONTROLS: Full-precision embeddings every round, parameter-sharing methods on the subset of users with congruent encoders, local training, total uploaded and downloaded bytes counted per user and round, and accuracy curves plotted against bytes rather than rounds, over three seeds.
COST: 160
PREDICTION: Compressed embeddings should reach most of the full-precision accuracy at a small fraction of the bytes of parameter sharing. Dense tasks may need finer embeddings than classification.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Compressing exchanged embeddings in representation-based federated learning
PROPOSAL: We compress the public-data embeddings exchanged in representation-based federated learning with random projection and quantisation, and report how accuracy changes for each heterogeneous user as compression increases, arguing that collaboration of this kind remains practical.
CONTROLS: Two random projection matrices drawn with different seeds, quantisation at two bit widths, an ablation of the projection dimension, accuracy curves plotted against rounds, and wall-clock time of the compression routine on the server.
COST: 160
PREDICTION: Accuracy should stay close to the uncompressed setting at moderate compression. Very low bit widths may hurt dense prediction users.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-modal federated users aligned through shared public pairs
PROPOSAL: Users working on images, text and audio each embed only their own modality of a public paired dataset, and the server aligns all modalities of the same instance jointly. We ask whether this improves each user's own task beyond local training, and whether it scales past two modalities where heuristic methods stop.
CONTROLS: Local training, pairwise alignment between modalities, the two-modality heuristic regulariser extended by summing pairwise terms, alignment with mismatched public pairs as placebo, and a two-modality subset to compare with the heuristic on its home ground.
COST: 380
PREDICTION: Every modality should gain over local training, with joint alignment ahead of summed pairwise terms. If mismatched pairs help as much, the gain is a regularisation effect.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated users in three modalities aligned on public paired data
PROPOSAL: Users working on images, text and audio each embed only their own modality of a public paired dataset, and the server aligns all modalities of the same instance jointly. We measure each user's task accuracy after collaboration and present the results for the three modalities and their combinations.
CONTROLS: Two public paired datasets of different size, two audio feature extractors, alignment run with and without a warm-up phase, an ablation of the server update frequency, and a qualitative look at retrieved neighbours across modalities.
COST: 380
PREDICTION: All three users should reach useful accuracy after collaboration. The audio user may benefit less since speech commands share little with captions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Effect of task relatedness on cross-task transfer in federated alignment
PROPOSAL: We vary relatedness between user tasks from identical to unrelated, using controlled splits of a large labelled image corpus, and measure the gain of joint representation alignment over local training as a function of relatedness and local data size, with heterogeneous backbones per user.
CONTROLS: Local training, a pooled centralised model, alignment on shuffled public data as placebo, a fixed-architecture variant to separate task from architecture effects, three seeds per configuration, and per-user confidence intervals.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: Gains should shrink as relatedness falls and vanish for unrelated tasks. Negative transfer for some users would show that alignment needs relatedness-aware weighting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task relatedness and accuracy in federated representation alignment
PROPOSAL: We vary relatedness between user tasks from identical to unrelated, using controlled splits of a large labelled image corpus, and record each user's accuracy under joint representation alignment for several local data sizes, with heterogeneous backbones per user.
CONTROLS: Two definitions of relatedness based on label overlap and on visual similarity, two orders of user arrival, an ablation of the public dataset domain, the alignment loss weight at two values, and training time per configuration.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: Accuracy should be higher for users with related tasks. Users with larger local datasets should reach higher accuracy in every configuration.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model-agnostic federated multi-task learning via joint embedding alignment
PROPOSAL: We let each user keep any architecture and any task, and exchange only embeddings of a shared unlabelled public dataset, which the server aligns jointly across all users with a total-correlation objective. Users add an alignment term to their local loss, so knowledge moves across tasks without sharing parameters or local data.
CONTROLS: Local training, pairwise contrastive alignment, distillation on public logits, a kernel alignment term, and a pooled centralised model, with per-user task metrics over three seeds.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: Most users should beat local training, and joint alignment should beat pairwise schemes with many users. Users on isolated tasks may gain little.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated multi-task learning through a shared pruned global model
PROPOSAL: We let each user extract a sub-network of a large global model sized to its resources, train it on its local task with its own head, and send updates of the shared sub-network weights to the server, which aggregates overlapping parameters. Knowledge then moves across tasks through the common global weights.
CONTROLS: Local training, pairwise contrastive alignment, distillation on public logits, a kernel alignment term, and a pooled centralised model, with per-user task metrics over three seeds.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: Most users should beat local training through shared weights. Users needing an architecture outside the global model family cannot take part.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Grounding joint alignment of many representations in total correlation
PROPOSAL: We derive a contrastive objective over the embeddings of one instance from all models as a variational bound on their total correlation, which captures dependence among all of them and not only between pairs, and we show how the existing Gramian loss arises as a special case. We validate on synthetic data with higher-order dependence and on multi-view benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Pairwise losses over all pairs, the Gramian loss, independent training, and synthetic data with only pairwise dependence.
COST: 220
PREDICTION: The derived loss should recover higher-order structure that pairwise losses miss. Bound looseness could hurt with high-dimensional embeddings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Aligning many representations through a shared anchor model
PROPOSAL: We designate one model as an anchor and align every other model's embeddings to the anchor with a pairwise contrastive loss, so the number of loss terms grows only linearly with the number of models, and we argue that alignment then propagates among all models through the anchor. We validate on synthetic data with higher-order dependence and on multi-view benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Pairwise losses over all pairs, the Gramian loss, independent training, and synthetic data with only pairwise dependence.
COST: 220
PREDICTION: Anchor alignment should match all-pairs alignment at lower cost of training. Models far from the anchor may align poorly with one another.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Collaboration across modalities without architectural congruity
PROPOSAL: We consider users with image, text and audio tasks who each embed only their own modality of a public paired dataset, and align all modalities of each public instance jointly on the server, so that knowledge transfers across tasks and modalities without sharing weights or local data, and without any limit of two modalities.
CONTROLS: Local training, pairwise alignment, the two-modality heuristic regulariser, mismatched public pairs as placebo, and per-user task metrics.
COST: 340
PREDICTION: All modalities should gain over local training. A small public paired set would limit the gains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Collaboration across modalities through a shared multimodal encoder
PROPOSAL: We give all users the same pretrained multimodal encoder, which each fine-tunes on its own modality and task, and average the encoder weights on the server each round, so that knowledge transfers across tasks and modalities through the common weights while local data stay on the device.
CONTROLS: Local training, pairwise alignment, the two-modality heuristic regulariser, averaging restricted to same-modality users, and per-user task metrics.
COST: 340
PREDICTION: All modalities should gain from the common encoder. Users who would prefer a smaller encoder cannot take part.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated alignment that scales to many users at low communication
PROPOSAL: We test whether joint embedding alignment stays practical as users grow from four to sixty-four, with partial participation, compressed public-data embeddings and a server loss whose computation grows linearly with users. We measure per-user accuracy, bytes exchanged and server computation per round against pairwise schemes that grow quadratically.
CONTROLS: Pairwise alignment, local training, uncompressed embeddings, and a fixed group of four users.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: Joint alignment should hold accuracy as users grow while traffic stays small. Very sparse participation may slow convergence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Federated alignment with a hierarchy of regional servers
PROPOSAL: We test whether adding regional servers that each aggregate a few users before forwarding to a central server keeps federated alignment practical, with users from four to sixty-four and partial participation. We measure per-user accuracy, latency between regions and server load per round against a flat topology with a single server.
CONTROLS: Pairwise alignment, local training, a flat topology, and a fixed group of four users.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: The hierarchy should lower central load as users grow. Users split across regions may align less well with each other.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge transfer across tasks for users of different foundation models
PROPOSAL: We simulate users who fine-tune different pretrained foundation models, from small convolutional networks to large vision transformers, on small local datasets for different tasks, and let them collaborate only through jointly aligned public-data embeddings. We test whether this improves every user's own task and lets small-model users benefit from large ones.
CONTROLS: Local fine-tuning, same-task distillation from the largest model, joint alignment with the large model frozen, and per-user metrics.
COST: 560
PREDICTION: Small-model users should gain the most without loss to large-model users. A wide capacity gap may limit how much small models can follow.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Selecting the best foundation model for each federated user
PROPOSAL: We simulate users who choose among pretrained foundation models, from small convolutional networks to large vision transformers, and design a server-side recommender that predicts which model each user should fine-tune given its task and resources. We test whether following the recommendations improves every user's own task over a random choice.
CONTROLS: Local fine-tuning with a random model, the largest model that fits each user, an oracle that tries all models, and per-user metrics.
COST: 560
PREDICTION: Recommended models should approach the oracle choice. Users with rare tasks may get poor recommendations.
